# In Context {#sec-in-context}

A lot of SEXP types feel mythical until the right expression manufactures
one. Absence from a typical script is not absence from the type system.
The notebook kept bumping into this, and it is worth walking type by type
with the context that makes each one show up.

## Builtins and specials

`typeof(sum)` is `"builtin"`. `typeof(`[`)` is `"special"`.
`typeof(`{`)` is `"special"`. `typeof(function() NULL)` is `"closure"`.
The nodes are `BUILTINSXP`, `SPECIALSXP`, and `CLOSXP`. They are easy to
miss because printing them shows `.Primitive("sum")` or the source of the
closure, and because you rarely `inspect` the function rather than the
value it returned.

The semantic difference is the old Lisp split between an applicative
function and a form that receives code. A builtin evaluates its arguments,
then receives the values. A special does not. `[`, `if`, `{`, `&&`, `||`,
`function`, `quote`, and `<-` have to be specials, because evaluating
everything first would destroy the construct. `` `&&` `` must not touch
the right-hand side when the left-hand side is false. `function` must not
evaluate the body at definition time. The internals manual calls these
out as
[special primitives](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html#Special-primitives).

Closures are the third kind: formals (a pairlist), body (usually a
`LANGSXP`), and enclosing environment. That triple is what `inspect`
prints under `FORMALS`, `BODY`, and `CLOENV`. An S7 class is one of these.
The notebook's `new_class()` dump is a `CLOSXP` with a class attribute of
`c("S7_class", "S7_object")` and a pile of metadata --- name, parent,
properties, validator, constructor --- hanging off the attribute pairlist.
The constructor you call is a function. The class object *is* that
function, plus attributes. That is a very R solution: reuse the closure
node you already have, and hang the dictionary off the side.

## Objects, factors, and the `integer64` lie

Two different words got called "object," and the confusion is reasonable.

`is.object(x)` answers the `OBJ` bit, which the header comment defines as
"does this have a class attribute?" A factor is an `INTSXP` with a
`levels` attribute and `class = "factor"`. The bit is set. `typeof` stays
`"integer"`. `OBJSXP` is a different question: type code 25, the node
shape used for S4 objects and for S7 instances, which do not consist
solely of a simple vector or function. The manual says so directly. The
notebook's S7 instance, after `@p <- "aaa"`, is type 25. The factor never
was.

Factors feel "more low-level" because base R and the C API know them
intimately: modeling code, tabulation, printing, `levels<-` as a
primitive generic. The representation pattern is still the S3 pattern.
Historically they had their own SEXP types, codes 11 and 12, and those
were withdrawn. The withdrawal is the tell. R decided that "integer plus
attributes" was enough type system for factors, and then lived with the
consequences.

`bit64::integer64()` is the same pattern with the costume showing.
`typeof` is `"double"`. Inspect shows a `REALSXP` with `OBJ` and `ATT`,
and a class string `"integer64"`. A double is 64 bits wide, so the
package stores a 64-bit integer in the payload a double would have used
and lies, politely, at the class layer. S3 as a reinterpretation of
storage is half of R's power. You can ship a new semantic type without a
new SEXPTYPE, which is why the set of SEXPTYPEs can stay frozen. It is
also half of R's pain. Every function that forgets to be generic will
treat the payload as what it physically is. `mean` of an `integer64`
without a method is a nonsense double. The class is law. The SEXPTYPE is
physics. Code that only knows physics will enforce physics.

`S7::class_any` is a useful decoy. Inspect shows a length-zero `VECSXP`
with class `"S7_any"`. It is not an S7 class constructor, and it is not an
`OBJSXP`. It is a base-type object used as a property constraint meaning
"anything." The slot exists so that a property can name its admitted
type. Leaving it at `class_any` is a choice, and @sec-types argues it is
usually the wrong one.

## Promises, dots, and byte code

You meet a `PROMSXP` by forcing the issue: `delayedAssign`, or inspecting
a formal while a call is live and the argument has not been touched. Dots
are `DOTSXP`, a pairlist of promises bound to `...`. Byte code is
`BCODESXP`. The compiler produces it, package loading produces it, and in
the S7 dumps the parent class `S7_object` already has a byte-coded body
because the package was built with the compiler on. You did not ask for
byte code. You asked for S7, and the namespace handed you a compiled
closure.

None of these require a debugger if you know which expression allocates
them. They do require you to stop expecting `inspect(1L)` to introduce
you to the whole zoo. The zoo comes to you when evaluation, compilation,
or a package constructor needs it.

## External pointers and weak references

These two get conflated because both smell like "systems programming,"
and they answer different questions.

| | External pointer | Weak reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | `EXTPTRSXP` | `WEAKREFSXP` |
| Manual's picture | a pointer, a protected R object, and a tag | a length-4 vector: key, value, finalizer, next |
| Job | name a foreign resource | remember a value only while the key is alive |
| Death | a finalizer can run when the pointer is collected | when the key dies, the weak reference clears and does not keep the key alive |

An external pointer is how an R object owns a GDAL dataset, a database
connection, a C++ instance. The R object is the handle you can name,
protect, and finalize. The bytes live in someone else's allocator.
`reg.finalizer` is the base-R hook for "run this when the node goes."
That is the interface principle from Chambers, made concrete: talking to
other languages includes talking about their lifetimes.

A weak reference is a cache that does not create a leak. The key is an
environment or an external pointer (or `NULL`). The value is what you
wanted to remember. The collector is allowed to forget the value when the
key is otherwise unreachable. Memoisation tables and package registries
use this so that "I have seen this object" does not become "I will keep
this object forever."

The user's complaint is correct and worth keeping. The C type being real
is not the same thing as a base constructor you can teach to a beginner.
`rlang::new_weakref` is a language-level wrapper. `typeof` on its result
is `"weakref"`, so once you hold one, R will admit the type exists.
Building one by hand is a C or package job. `reg.finalizer` is the piece
base actually exports for the neighboring problem. A lot of "tidyverse
primitives" have this shape: the runtime grew the capability, and a
package grew the API. ALTREP classes, a comfortable restart surface, and
weak maps all sit in that gap. Internals are not the standard library.
Pretending they are is how people tell you the feature "already exists"
when what exists is a struct.

## S7 values and R6 handles, at the level of nodes

This is the identity fork, photographed.

An S7 class object is a `CLOSXP`. Calling it allocates an instance. In
the notebook the instance is an `OBJSXP` whose attributes carry the class
string and a pointer back at the class. Properties live in that
structure. `@p <-` went through a replacement function and the address
changed. Same physics as `df$x <-` on a data frame: value semantics,
copy-on-modify, a new node for the modified object. The class object
itself is shared. Instances point back at it. Dispatch is generic
functions, not messages stored in the instance.

An R6 generator is an `ENVSXP`. The dump is a guided tour of a mutable
dictionary: a hash table, bindings for `classname` and `public_fields`,
closures whose enclosing environment is the generator itself, a `clone`
method whose body builds new environments and remaps closures into them,
`lockEnvironment`, `reg.finalizer` wired to `$finalize`, and the famous
`.__enclos_env__` chain. Methods are closures closed over the object
environment. That is the Scheme model of an object, shipped as a package.
`$foo <-` does not change the address. Cloning is an explicit walk. The
giant paste in the notebook is the clone machinery's source, seen from
the inside, and it is allowed to be ugly. It is doing something the
value world gets for free.

S7's experimental `class_environment` is the admission that the class
machinery and the identity regime are separable. You can ask for S7's
properties and validators on environment physics. The documentation marks
it dangerous because it *is* dangerous: you have opted out of the value
illusion while keeping a syntax that looks like the illusion. Use it when
you mean a handle. Do not use it because an environment seemed like a
convenient list.

## What the physics does not decide

Knowing that an instance is an `OBJSXP` does not tell you whether `color`
should be a class. It tells you that if you make it an S7 value, property
replacement will behave like data-frame replacement, and if you make it
an R6 object, property replacement will behave like environment
assignment. The physics constrains the promises you can keep. The
vocabulary is still your job. That is the hinge into the second half of
the book.
